title: Mostly Martha
full_review:
An uptight professional chef has her orderly world turned into an upside-down cake in the tasty German romantic comedy �Mostly Martha� (Paramount Classics).

Although Germany is not the first place one would think of to inspire culinary delights, writer-director Sandra Nettelbeck�s film does just that, combining an old-fashioned romance with tantalizing scenes of gastronomic enchantment. Martina Gedeck is Martha, the head chef at a prestigious Munich restaurant where she runs the kitchen with an iron ladle. Cool and stern, Martha does not suffer culinary fools easily. She verbally attacks any customer who attempts to send her food back.

The story is another installment in the blossoming subgenre of food movies such as Ang Lee�s �Eat Drink Man Woman,� Gabriel Axel�s �Babette�s Feast� or Stanley Tucci�s �Big Night.� The film is more than just an epicurean extravaganza, although the scenes of the bustling restaurant kitchen with its sauces simmering and exquisite dishes meticulously prepared and resembling works or art are mouth watering.

�Mostly Martha� is not the most original recipe, yet it has a bittersweet, philosophical edge that is appealing. Nettelbeck shows real affection for her characters, despite -� or maybe because of �- their foibles, and warmly invites the audience to do the same. Martha�s solitary life unexpectedly changes when her 8-year-old niece, Lina (Maxime Foerste), comes to live with her after a family tragedy. Lina is very much like Martha: a stubborn introvert who doesn�t like change. Even worse, Lina refuses to eat, which cuts off the only way �- food -- Martha knows how to communicate with people. (Martha even uses cuisine as a means to deflect her therapist�s questions, hoping to distract him with her extraordinary dishes.)

Just as Martha tries to balance her new parenting responsibilities, she is thrown another ball to juggle. Without her knowledge, Martha�s restaurant boss (Sibylle Canonica) hires charismatic sous-chef Mario (Sergio Castellitto). Mario�s flamboyant style adds not only new cooking elements to the kitchen, but with Italian songs blaring in the background, he also adds joy and laughter to what was once a quiet, and dull, atmosphere. Their contrasting techniques are only too evident, pushing Martha to make more than her usual frequent trips to the restaurant�s freezer when things get too hot and hectic.

The turning point comes when Mario breaks Lina�s virtual hunger strike by feeding her some delicious pasta. Martha suddenly sees Mario, who was initially viewed as an intruder, in a different light and it opens the door to romantic possibilities. Mario also opens Martha�s eyes to a life filled with joy and love, despite the risk of pain. Gedeck and Castellitto have such a convincing and attractive rapport that it is hard to believe that neither was speaking the same language during filming. Not knowing a word of German, Castellitto spoke all his lines in Italian, which were then dubbed into German.

�Mostly Martha� is a tragic comedy that pleases. Nettelbeck brings together the many varying story elements, including a plot strand about locating Lina�s Italian father, in a satisfying manner. Her tale urges audiences not to settle for fast food when a gourmet meal is there for the taking.

Because of romantic complications and fleeting crass language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
